references.text: The disciples did not understand this word when Jesus spoke about his coming suffering, and they were afraid to ask him – a direct parallel to Luke's account.
Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' second prediction of his suffering, where the disciples became very sorrowful but did not fully grasp what Jesus meant.
Here too, the listeners (Mary and Joseph) did not understand the word Jesus spoke to them – a similar motif of failing to comprehend Jesus' words.
The preceding verse where Jesus predicts that the Son of Man will be handed over into human hands – this is the ῥῆμα (word) that the disciples did not understand.
At the third prediction of suffering, it is again explicitly stated that the disciples understood none of this, and the meaning was hidden from them – nearly identical wording.
The Gospel of John confirms that the disciples did not understand these things at first, but only after Jesus' glorification did they grasp what had been written about him.
The disciples ask one another what Jesus means and do not understand his words – again an example showing that Jesus' predictions about his departure were hidden from them.
The first prediction of suffering in Mark, where Peter rebukes Jesus – a sign that the disciples did not understand the necessity of Jesus' suffering and death.
After the resurrection, Jesus opens the disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures concerning his suffering – what had previously been hidden from them (as in 9:45) was now revealed.
Jesus opened their minds so they could understand the Scriptures that the Messiah must suffer – a direct fulfillment and clarification of the lack of understanding described in 9:45.
